title: The five virtues
hookLine: truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love guard the same house

cards: An unlocked back door, and five thieves already inside. So what do you do? Buy a bigger lock?
Sit up all night with a flashlight, glaring at every shadow? People try that with their own minds: white-knuckle willpower, fighting every bad impulse head-on. It's exhausting, and it rarely lasts.
Now think of a house that feels safe. Usually it isn't safe because of locks. It's safe because of who lives there: people who are kind, honest, settled, glad to be home.
Thieves don't like a full, lit, busy house. The Granth's answer to the five thieves is five guards.

teach.b: Sikh teaching names five virtues. Sat: truth, being true all the way through. Santokh: contentment, the enough you met in Pauri 10.
Daya: compassion. Nimrata: humility. And pyaar: love.
An honest note: you won't find these five printed as a numbered list on one page of the Granth.

The list is a way Sikh teachers gather what the Granth says across hundreds of hymns, and each of the five is everywhere in it. You've already heard them in the Japji. Pauri 16: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot.
The bull that holds up the earth is dharma, the child of compassion, and contentment is in the next line too, though commentators read its exact role there in more than one way.
Pauri 18, Guru Nanak calling himself lowly: humility. Pauri 21: listening, trusting, and love in the mind. And sach, truth, from the Mool Mantar on.
Many Sikh teachers pair each guard with a thief. Humility stands against pride. Compassion against anger.
Contentment against greed. Love, wide and giving, against attachment that clings. And truth against lust, desire that grabs what isn't true to the moment.
The guards don't beat the thieves in a fistfight.
When humility is home, pride has no room to sit down. So instead of staring at the shadows all night, you practice one guard, and the house slowly changes who lives in it.

how: Sikhs are commonly taught the five virtues, sat, santokh, daya, nimrata and pyaar, alongside the five thieves, and many teachers pair each virtue with the thief it answers.

games.q: each guard and its thief — tap the pairs.

s: the five virtues appear as a numbered list on one page of the Granth
Sikh teachers gather them from across the Granth, where each appears again and again.
Japji 16 calls dharma the child of compassion
the guards beat the thieves by force
they fill the house, so the thieves have no room.

games.q: pride keeps walking into your house. which guard do many Sikh teachers set against it?
games.why: nimrata, humility, stands against ahankaar, pride. when humility is home, pride has nowhere to sit.

practice: Think of yesterday's thief, the one most active in you, and find its guard: for anger, compassion; for greed, contentment; for pride, humility; for clinging, a wider love; for grabbing, truth.
Picture that guard standing at your door, calm and awake. Breathe it in to fill your chest, and out to fill the room, a house filling with light.

wordCard.voice: Nimrata, humility. Truth, contentment, compassion, nimrata and love: gathered from across the Granth, five guards for the same house the thieves live in.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the five virtues, truth, contentment, compassion, humility, love.

carryVoice: Your line: five guards at the door. Truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love. Day two hundred forty, in the books.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3–4 (Japji, Pauris 10, 18 and 21)
